summaries.example: Imagine a group of students solving puzzles with the same set of rules and tools. At first, the puzzles seem manageable. If many puzzles cannot be solved, the students may lose trust in their usual method. Someone might suggest a new set of rules. The new method could solve many problems, but it might also make some old answers unusable. Kuhn thought science can change in a similar way.
summaries.summary: Thomas Kuhn studied how science really changes by looking closely at its history. He argued that science is not always a smooth pile of new facts. For long stretches, scientists work within a shared model, or paradigm. This is normal science: they solve puzzles using familiar ideas, tools, and examples. Sometimes troubling problems, called anomalies, collect. If confidence in the old model weakens, a crisis can begin. Scientists may then adopt a rival model in a scientific revolution. The new model can solve important puzzles, but it may not keep every old solution. Kuhn called this loss of some earlier achievements “Kuhn-loss.” He also argued that scientists working with different paradigms may use different standards, notice different features, and use important words differently. This makes comparison difficult, though not always impossible. Kuhn’s view still allows science to make progress: later science can solve more and more detailed problems without necessarily moving toward one final description of reality.
key_ideas: Science usually has long periods of puzzle-solving called normal science.
When important problems build up, scientists may enter a crisis and consider a new paradigm.
A new paradigm can solve important problems but may also leave some older achievements behind.
Kuhn said scientific progress does not have to mean moving ever closer to one perfect final theory.
What scientists notice and how they describe it can be influenced by their training and theories.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kuhn helps us understand why changing a scientific idea can be difficult. People do not judge every idea with completely neutral rules; their training gives them examples of what counts as a good problem and a good solution. His work also reminds us to study the history of science instead of assuming that older scientists were simply foolish. Thinking about Kuhn can make us more careful when we hear that science always grows in a perfectly straight line.

important_terms.definition: A shared model that guides scientists. It gives them puzzles to work on and examples of good ways to solve them.
The everyday work scientists do when they use an accepted model to solve familiar problems.
A major change in the shared model used by a scientific community.
A serious problem that the usual scientific model has trouble explaining.
A situation in which two theories cannot be measured or compared by exactly the same standards.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people look at the same event and notice different things because they expect different things?
Would you always choose a new method if it solved some problems but made an old answer harder to use?
What makes a scientific change a helpful improvement?
Can people disagree reasonably even when they share many rules and goals?

summaries.example: Consider the transition from older physics to Einstein’s relativity. A common view says that Newton’s theory remains a special, approximately correct case of Einstein’s theory. Kuhn’s analysis raises a deeper problem: terms such as “mass” do not necessarily have exactly the same role or meaning in the two theoretical frameworks. Even if the theories can be compared in some respects, the standards and conceptual network used for comparison have changed. This illustrates why scientific change can involve both improvement in problem-solving and difficulty in judging one theory from the standpoint of another.
summaries.summary: Thomas Kuhn’s philosophy of science developed from historical studies of physics and astronomy. His central account describes alternating periods of normal science and scientific revolution. During normal science, a community works within a disciplinary matrix: a shared arrangement of theories, instruments, techniques, values, and metaphysical assumptions. Paradigms, in the narrower sense, are exemplary achievements that teach scientists how to recognize puzzles, approach them, and assess proposed solutions. This practice is not governed entirely by explicit algorithms. Anomalies are often tolerated, but a sufficiently serious accumulation can produce a crisis. A rival framework may then be adopted, changing the problems considered central, the methods used, and sometimes the meanings of important terms. Kuhn called the resulting difficulty of comparison incommensurability. He distinguished methodological incommensurability, arising from changing standards; observational incommensurability, arising from theory-shaped perception and evidence; and semantic incommensurability, arising from changes in interconnected vocabularies and taxonomies. He did not mean that rival theories are wholly incomparable. Scientists still share values including accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, and fruitfulness, though these values are imprecise and can conflict. Kuhn’s account permits progress, but interprets it mainly as increased problem-solving power, complexity, and specialization rather than as guaranteed convergence on one complete true theory.
key_ideas: Kuhn contrasts normal science with revolutionary science rather than treating revolutions as simply faster progress.
Scientific communities are guided by paradigms understood as exemplary problem-solutions, not only by explicit rules.
A crisis develops when important anomalies threaten the ability of normal science to continue confidently.
Theory choice is constrained by values such as accuracy, consistency, scope, simplicity, and fruitfulness, but these values do not mechanically determine one answer.
Incommensurability has methodological, observational, and semantic forms; Kuhn’s account of semantic incommensurability changed over his career.
Kuhn’s evolutionary picture allows genuine scientific progress through greater problem-solving power and specialization without requiring progress toward a final, unified theory.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kuhn changed how philosophers examine scientific rationality, evidence, and historical change. His account challenges the idea that science advances by applying permanent, theory-independent rules to neutral observations. At the same time, it should not be reduced to the claim that science is irrational or that every scientific choice is determined by society. Kuhn emphasizes internal scientific considerations while allowing room for disagreement when shared values underdetermine a decision. His work therefore provides a framework for studying both the stability of expert communities and the conceptual disruption produced by major changes in science.

important_terms.definition: In Kuhn’s narrower and especially important sense, an exemplary scientific achievement that provides models for identifying, approaching, and judging later puzzles.
Research carried out within a disciplinary matrix, where shared theories, instruments, values, techniques, and examples guide puzzle-solving.
A period in which an established disciplinary matrix is revised or replaced, rather than merely extended through ordinary puzzle-solving.
A persistent or especially serious problem that strains confidence in the existing disciplinary matrix.
The difficulty of comparing theories because their methods, observations, or languages may lack a single common measure.
The view that what scientists observe is partly shaped by prior concepts, training, and theoretical expectations.
Kuhn’s later account in which scientific terms form changing classificatory systems whose categories may not translate neatly across major theory changes.

questions_to_think_about: If accuracy, simplicity, and scope conflict, can a fixed rule decide which value should matter most?
Does theory-dependent observation show that evidence is subjective, or only that evidence is interpreted within a framework?
Can two theories be meaningfully compared even when they are not fully translatable?
Does solving more and more sophisticated puzzles count as progress if it does not mean becoming closer to truth?
How might training with examples shape a scientist’s ability to recognize a new solution?

summaries.example: Suppose your school uses one app to organize all homework. Students learn its buttons, shortcuts, and usual ways of fixing problems. If a few assignments fail to upload, teachers may treat them as glitches. But if the failures keep spreading, the school may face a crisis. It might replace the app with another system. The new system could handle the biggest problems better, yet some old features or saved methods might disappear. Students using the two systems could also describe the same task differently. This is similar to Kuhn’s picture of normal science, crisis, and revolution.
summaries.summary: Thomas Kuhn argued that science changes in a pattern more complicated than “new facts are added to old facts.” A scientific community usually works within a shared framework. Kuhn called this normal science. Researchers use the framework’s theories, instruments, methods, values, and examples to solve puzzles. A paradigm, especially in Kuhn’s later clarification, is an exemplary achievement that shows how to recognize and solve similar puzzles. This shared training helps scientists make progress, but it also makes them cautious about challenging the framework. Strange results, or anomalies, may be ignored or explained away. If serious anomalies multiply and normal research loses confidence, a crisis can develop. A rival framework may then bring a scientific revolution. Such a change is not simply an improved version of ordinary research. It can alter which problems matter, how evidence is interpreted, and how important terms are used. Kuhn called the resulting difficulty of comparison incommensurability. He discussed methodological differences, theory-shaped observation, and changes in scientific language and classification. Still, he did not say that theories cannot be compared at all or that scientific choices are random. Scientists commonly value accuracy, consistency, broad scope, simplicity, and usefulness for future research. These values guide judgment, but they can be interpreted and balanced differently. For Kuhn, progress is real when science becomes better at solving important and increasingly specialized problems, even if this does not prove that it is moving toward one final truth.
key_ideas: Kuhn says science has both stable periods and disruptive periods, not just a steady accumulation of facts.
During normal science, researchers usually protect the basic framework and work on puzzles it makes possible.
Anomalies do not automatically destroy a theory; many are set aside until they become serious enough to cause a crisis.
Scientific revolutions can change standards, observations, vocabulary, and the kinds of problems scientists see as important.
Different frameworks may be difficult to compare, but they can still overlap in some ways and share scientific values.
Science can progress by gaining problem-solving power without necessarily approaching one final theory of everything.
summaries.why_it_matters: Kuhn’s ideas help explain why experts can disagree during major changes without one side being obviously foolish. They also show why scientific evidence is not always a completely neutral referee: people trained in different frameworks may notice and interpret things differently. His approach encourages us to connect philosophy with the history of science. At the same time, Kuhn’s own position is more careful than the claim that facts do not matter. Scientific communities remain constrained by problem-solving success and shared values, even when those constraints do not determine a single unavoidable choice.

important_terms.definition: A shared scientific framework that gives researchers examples, tools, questions, and ways to judge proposed solutions.
The routine research done inside an accepted framework, usually by solving puzzles rather than questioning the framework itself.
A major change in which one scientific framework is replaced or revised so that difficult problems can be addressed.
A puzzling result that does not fit easily with the accepted framework.
A lack of one complete standard for comparing theories from different scientific frameworks.
The idea that what counts as an observation can depend partly on a person’s previous ideas, training, and expectations.
A group’s shared commitments about theories, tools, values, methods, and examples; Kuhn sometimes used this phrase instead of the broader word “paradigm.”

questions_to_think_about: Why might scientists ignore a surprising result for a while instead of immediately rejecting their main theory?
Can a new framework be better even if it does not preserve every success of the older one?
If two groups use different meanings for a key word, what would they need to do to understand one another?
Are shared values like simplicity and accuracy enough to settle every scientific disagreement?
What might be gained by studying the history of science when deciding what science is like today?
